common_name: Crimson Beauty Moss Phlox (Deep Rose-Red Creeping Phlox)

planting.note: Plant in well-drained to dry, lean soil in full sun; Crimson Beauty is a long-grown moss phlox selection prized for flowers that read a deeper rose-red than the more common lavender-blue or pink shades of the species.

directions: Crimson Beauty covers its needle-like evergreen foliage each spring in a dense sheet of rose-red, star-shaped flowers, one of the deepest warm reds among moss phlox selections. Site it in lean, sharply drained soil in full sun, such as a rock garden, dry slope, or wall crevice, since damp winter soil around the crown quickly leads to rot. Shear the mat back lightly right after flowering to keep growth tight and to push a fresh flush of foliage for the rest of the season. Established plants form a durable, drought-tolerant evergreen carpet that needs little care beyond an occasional post-bloom trim.

common_name: Atropurpurea Moss Phlox (Dark Purple-Red Creeping Phlox)

planting.note: Plant in well-drained to dry, lean soil in full sun; Atropurpurea is an old moss phlox selection named for its unusually dark, purple-tinged red flower color.

directions: Atropurpurea is a long-established moss phlox selection whose small star-shaped flowers open in a smoldering, purple-tinted red distinct from the brighter pinks and blues typical of the species, smothering the evergreen, needle-like foliage each spring. Grow it in lean, gritty, sharply drained soil in full sun, the same conditions the wild species favors on rocky slopes, and avoid heavy or poorly drained ground that invites crown rot over winter. Shear the mat lightly after the flowers fade to keep the growth dense and tidy through summer. It spreads slowly into a low, evergreen carpet well suited to rock gardens, dry walls, and border edges.

common_name: Ronsdorf Beauty Moss Phlox (Deep Pink Creeping Phlox)

planting.note: Plant in well-drained to dry, lean soil in full sun; Ronsdorf Beauty is a German-raised moss phlox selection grown for deep pink flowers set off by a darker central eye.

directions: Ronsdorf Beauty carries dense clusters of deep rose-pink, star-shaped flowers, each marked with a slightly darker eye, held tight against a needle-like evergreen mat in mid-spring. Give it lean, sharply drained soil in full sun, as excess fertility or wet feet through winter both push the mat toward rot and floppy, open growth. Shear the plant back lightly once flowering finishes to renew dense foliage and keep the mound from becoming woody and sparse in the center. Its trailing, mat-forming habit makes it a reliable choice for cascading over rock walls, edging dry borders, or covering sunny slopes.

common_name: Prime Minister Garden Phlox (White with Red Eye)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in rich, moist, well-drained soil in full sun; Prime Minister is a long-established English garden phlox valued for its clean white flowers centered by a contrasting red-purple eye.

directions: Prime Minister is an old-fashioned garden phlox that has stayed in cultivation for generations on the strength of its large, domed flower trusses: pure white petals surrounding a small but vivid red-purple eye. Grow it in fertile, evenly moist, well-drained soil in full sun, and space plants generously to keep air moving through the foliage, which helps limit the powdery mildew that troubles many garden phlox in humid summers. Deadhead spent flower heads to prolong bloom and prevent unwanted seedlings, since seed-grown phlox rarely comes true to the parent's coloring. The strong stems and bold flower color make it a dependable middle-to-back-of-border perennial and a good cut flower.

common_name: Mount Fuji Garden Phlox (Tall Pure White Phlox)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in rich, moist, well-drained soil in full sun; Mount Fuji is a tall, long-cultivated garden phlox grown for its dense trusses of pure white flowers.

directions: Mount Fuji sends up sturdy, upright stems topped with large, rounded trusses of unmarked, snow-white flowers, one of the purest whites among tall garden phlox and a classic choice for the back of a summer border. Plant it in rich, consistently moist, well-drained soil in full sun, and thin crowded clumps every few years to improve air circulation, since dense stands of white garden phlox are especially prone to powdery mildew in humid weather. Deadhead as flowers fade to extend the bloom season and stop the plant from setting seed that reverts to muddy magenta seedlings. Its height and clean color make it a strong companion for dark-leaved perennials or as a light-catching accent at dusk.

common_name: The King Garden Phlox (Deep Violet-Blue Phlox)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in rich, moist, well-drained soil in full sun; The King is an early-blooming, long-established English garden phlox grown for its deep violet-blue flower color.

directions: The King bears rounded clusters of richly saturated violet-blue flowers, among the deepest true blues available in garden phlox, and tends to open earlier in the season than many other paniculata cultivars. Grow it in fertile, evenly moist, well-drained soil in full sun, giving plants room to breathe so foliage dries quickly after rain and stays cleaner through the humid stretch of summer that favors powdery mildew. Cut spent flower trusses back to a side shoot to encourage a secondary flush of bloom later in the season. Its relatively compact height and intense color work well toward the middle of a mixed perennial border, paired with silver foliage or pale yellow companions to set off the blue.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in rich, moist, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Harlequin is an older garden phlox grown as much for its cream-margined variegated foliage as for its purple-violet flowers.

directions: Harlequin pairs the reliable purple-violet flower trusses of a classic garden phlox with strongly cream-edged, variegated foliage that gives the clump ornamental interest well before and after the midsummer bloom period. Grow it in rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil, siting it in full sun to light afternoon shade, where the leaf margins tend to hold their brightness without scorching. Watch for any all-green reversion shoots on the clump and cut them out at the base promptly, since they grow more vigorously than the variegated stems and will overtake the plant if left. Divide congested clumps every few years in spring to maintain vigor and the clean variegation that makes this cultivar distinctive among garden phlox.

common_name: Windsor Garden Phlox (Carmine-Rose Phlox with Red Eye)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in rich, moist, well-drained soil in full sun; Windsor is a long-established English garden phlox grown for carmine-rose flowers centered on a deeper red eye.

directions: Windsor carries broad, domed trusses of vivid carmine-rose flowers, each accented by a small, darker red eye, on sturdy, well-branched stems through the heat of midsummer. Plant it in fertile, consistently moist, well-drained soil in full sun, and space clumps generously to promote airflow that helps keep powdery mildew in check during humid weather. Deadhead faded trusses to keep the display tidy and to push a further round of bloom later in the season. Its saturated warm-pink color reads well from a distance, making it a reliable anchor for the middle of a sunny summer border.
